title: Blood and Guts program review
summary: NH reviews Dorian Yates' Blood and Guts HIT program on its parameters alone and rejects it for naturals: one hard set plus forced reps sacrifices tonnage, raises injury risk at the bottom of negatives, and leaves biceps, calves, legs, forearms, traps and abs undertrained. He also flags poor exercise ordering, too few warm-ups and misnamed lifts.
claims: Judge a program by its sets, reps and exercise selection, never by its creator's fame or physique
Blood and Guts is a 6-week, 4-day body part split resembling two upper and two lower days, trained two on, one off
A program labeled high intensity is really a low-volume program; bodybuilding needs both values, not an extreme of one
How intensity is programmed matters as much as how much; a supposedly high-intensity program can produce no hypertrophy
Doing only one hard set per exercise wastes the highest-quality tonnage; you want to multiply hard sets
Forced reps need a partner and suit machines and presses; they barely work for squats, deadlifts or rows
Copying enhanced lifters' programs is misleading because you cannot tell whether growth came from the stimulus or the drugs
A 10-minute treadmill warm-up is useless; warm up with the lift itself
Needing rotator cuff isolation before pressing suggests poor pressing form; understandable when old, abnormal at 25
Two warm-up sets for a heavy first exercise are too few; do as many as you need, and warm-ups still add volume to an already low-volume program
A 6-8 rep range with no set evolution gives a tiny progression window and mostly guarantees easy success rather than progression
Flies suit high reps, multiple sets and supersets, not one heavy set
Concentration curls do not suit a heavy one-set style, and Dorian's curl form was sloppy
If the bar rises to shoulder height in a curl it becomes a front raise, shifting work to the shoulders
Chest and biceps is not a synergistic pairing
Two hard biceps sets a week will not grow trained arms; forced reps only artificially inflate intensity, and four hard sets three times a week would blow it away
A 'back day' always works arms or the posterior chain too, so name the day accordingly
Pullovers are excellent but should not be trained at high intensity; the weak link is the shoulders and elbows, not the lats, so multiply sets instead
Naturals should do pull-ups over pulldowns: better for hypertrophy, spinal decompression and shoulder health; pros avoid them because of their poor strength-to-size ratio
Deadlifts belong at the start as strength work; at the end of a back day a fatigued thoracic extension raises injury risk and weakens leg drive
One warm-up set before a heavy deadlift is unrealistic, e.g. jumping from 200 to 400 lb
Dorian's 'deadlift' is actually an RDL; 8-10 reps is too high for conventional or sumo deadlifts but a good range for RDLs
The back day hammers the lats while barely touching traps and rhomboids
Big legs as a natural require training them often and hard
One high-intensity set of lateral raises is unwise for the delicate shoulder; dumbbell plus cable laterals are redundant and exist only to honor the program's philosophy
Machines lock movement to one axis, causing unnatural patterns and possible imbalances; pullover and pulldown machines pulling across the body risk biceps injury
99% of injuries happen at the bottom of the negative while reversing into the positive; forced reps extend time spent there
Lifts differ in their ratio of stress on the structure to stress on the muscle; forced reps have a poor ratio and cannot replace sets
Triceps are small and respond to high frequency; nucleus overload works well for them
Big muscle groups lean toward strength work, small ones toward volume; small muscles are easier to overtrain and injure
One heavy hard set of skull crushers will wreck your elbows
Training legs once a week on a dedicated leg day applies frequency terribly; one of every two days should include a knee flexion or hip hinge
Needing a long stretching routine to squat or deadlift signals a problem
Leg extensions are the cherry on top; legs grow from squats and deadlifts, and one heavy set of extensions just hurts the knee
Do not do leg press and hack squat on the same day; pick one, progress it, rotate if bored
The leg curl is the lift best suited to negatives and forced reps
A true stiff-leg deadlift starts from a dead stop; most people do a stiff-legged RDL instead
Calves are stubborn because you walk on them all day, so one working set will not grow them; the rest-pause sets show Dorian knew this
The program has no forearm, trap or ab isolation; naturals must isolate lagging muscles, and enhanced claims they grow anyway are false
Fans gain on it because it forces them to train to failure and isolate arms for the first time, a new stimulus
The program is built to progress fast then crash; bodybuilders should seek a program they can stay on as long as possible rather than 6-week blocks
He does not recommend it even as a HIT or strength cycle; program strength work and hard sets instead
